This guide walks through the package with a small, real data set. Every
output below is produced by the installed package when this page is built.

## Installation

```{r}
#| eval: false
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("jaxsonbugg/nbzinbreg")
```

```{r}
library(nbzinbreg)
```

## The Data

The examples use `bioChemists` from the pscl package: the number of articles
(`art`) published by 915 biochemistry PhD students in the last three years of
their PhD, with gender (`fem`), marital status (`mar`), the number of children
under 6 (`kid5`), the prestige of the PhD programme (`phd`) and the number of
articles by the student's mentor (`ment`).

```{r}
data("bioChemists", package = "pscl")
c(mean = mean(bioChemists$art), variance = var(bioChemists$art),
  zeros = mean(bioChemists$art == 0))
```

The variance is more than twice the mean (overdispersion), which a Poisson
model cannot describe.

## Negative Binomial Regression

`nbreg()` takes a formula and a data frame, like `glm()`. The coefficients
are on the log scale of the expected count; `theta` is the dispersion
parameter, with variance $\mu + \mu^2/\theta$.

```{r}
fit_nb <- nbreg(art ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment, data = bioChemists)
summary(fit_nb)
```

`exp(coef(fit_nb))` gives incidence rate ratios: the factor by which the
expected count changes per unit of a covariate.

```{r}
round(exp(coef(fit_nb)), 3)
```

## Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Regression

`zinbreg()` adds a second, logistic model for the probability of a
*structural zero* (a student who would publish nothing in any case). The
formula has two parts: count covariates before `|`, zero covariates after.
Without `|`, both parts use the same covariates.

```{r}
fit_zi <- zinbreg(art ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment | ment,
                  data = bioChemists)
summary(fit_zi)
```

The summary also reports how the fit converged: the number of EM
iterations and the gradient check at the estimates.

## Comparing the Models

`logLik()` carries the number of parameters, so `AIC()` and `BIC()` work
directly.

```{r}
c(AIC_nb = AIC(fit_nb), AIC_zinb = AIC(fit_zi),
  BIC_nb = BIC(fit_nb), BIC_zinb = BIC(fit_zi))
```

`overdispersion_test()` tests the Poisson model against NB, and
`vuong_test()` compares the ZINB and NB fits. Because NB is the boundary of
ZINB, the Vuong statistics are descriptive; `vuong_test(B = 199)` adds a
parametric bootstrap test (it refits both models for every replicate, so it
takes a while).

```{r}
overdispersion_test(fit_nb)
vuong_test(fit_zi, fit_nb)
```

## Predictions

`predict()` gives the expected count, and for ZINB also the count-part mean,
the probability of a structural zero, or the probability of each count. It
accepts `newdata`, and `se.fit = TRUE` adds delta-method standard errors.

```{r}
new <- data.frame(fem = c("Men", "Women"), mar = "Married", kid5 = 0,
                  phd = 3, ment = 10)
predict(fit_zi, newdata = new, type = "response")
predict(fit_zi, newdata = new, type = "zero")
round(predict(fit_zi, newdata = new, type = "prob")[, 1:4], 3)
```

## Confidence Intervals

`confint()` gives Wald intervals for the coefficients and a
profile-likelihood interval for theta.

```{r}
confint(fit_nb)
```

## Diagnostics

`expected_counts()` compares observed and expected frequencies of each count,
and `rootogram()` draws them as a hanging rootogram: bars that end below the
dashed line are counts the model under-predicts.

```{r}
head(expected_counts(fit_zi), 5)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
rootogram(fit_zi, max_count = 12)
```

## Control Settings

`nbreg_control()` and `zinbreg_control()` set tolerances and iteration
limits, and `trace = TRUE` prints the progress of the fit. For ZINB,
`hessian = "numeric"` uses a numerical Hessian for the standard errors
instead of the analytic one.

```{r}
fit_zi_num <- zinbreg(art ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment | ment,
                      data = bioChemists,
                      control = zinbreg_control(hessian = "numeric"))
max(abs(sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_zi_num))) - sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_zi)))))
```

## Tidy Summaries

`tidy()` and `glance()` return the coefficient table and the model summary
as data frames.

```{r}
head(tidy(fit_zi), 4)
glance(fit_zi)
```
